title: Gastrointestinal distress is common during a 161-km ultramarathon
population: 272 finishers and non-finishers of the 161-km Western States Endurance Run (71.0% of starters), post-race questionnaire
findings: 96.0% of runners reported at least one GI symptom; flatulence (65.9%), belching (61.3%) and nausea (60.3%) were the most common.
Among finishers, 43.9% said GI symptoms affected race performance, nausea being the most common (86.0%).
Among non-finishers, 35.6% said GI symptoms were a reason for dropping out, nausea being the most common (90.5%).
Nausea was greatest during the most challenging and hottest part of the race.
272 runners (71.0% of starters) completed the questionnaire; 96.0% experienced GI symptoms.
Most common: flatulence (65.9%), belching (61.3%) and nausea (60.3%), each mean severity about 1.0 on the 0-4 scale.
Among finishers, 43.9% said GI symptoms affected performance (nausea 86.0% of those); among non-finishers 35.6% said GI symptoms were a reason for dropping out (nausea 90.5%).
limitations: Retrospective self-report from one race; symptoms are not experimentally linked to diet or training; no intervention tested.
implications: Make gut-tolerance rehearsal a standing element of the 100-mile build (practise planned race fuel in long runs, ideally including hot sessions) because GI distress is near-universal and a major cited reason for dropping out.
Use nausea as a prompt in race-day guidance for pace reduction and a fuelling plan change, not as a signal to quit by default.
Expect GI symptoms and plan for them (backup foods, savoury options, reduced pace in heat), not as failures.
Use nausea in heat as a trigger to reduce intensity and switch to simple fuel; include a hot-segment contingency in race notes.
Log GI symptoms in training long runs on the same 0-4 scale.

verification.notes: Added in this review for DNF reasons. Crossref (2015-02-26, first author Stuempfle, Journal of Sports Sciences) and Europe PMC abstract (PMID 25716739) fetched; all numbers stated in the abstract.
